items.question: Why is tungsten used for making filaments of electric bulbs?

options.B: It has high resistivity and very high melting point
options.C: It is a good conductor of electricity

items.answer: B
items.explanation: Tungsten has a very high melting point (3380 degrees C) so it does not melt even at the high temperatures needed to emit light. It also has appreciable resistivity (5.20 x 10^-8 Omega m) to produce sufficient heat. Option A (low melting point) is wrong - tungsten has very high melting point.

items.question: The heat produced in a conductor of resistance R when current I flows for time t is H = I^2 x R x t. If the same power is dissipated in two resistors R and 2R connected in series, what is the ratio of heat produced in R to heat produced in 2R?
items.answer: B
items.explanation: In series, same current I flows through both. H_R = I^2 x R x t; H_2R = I^2 x 2R x t. Ratio = H_R/H_2R = R/(2R) = 1/2, i.e., 1:2. More heat in 2R than in R for same current. Options C and D are reversed or incorrect.

subtopics.subtopic_name: PRACTICAL APPLICATIONS OF HEATING EFFECT OF ELECTRIC CURRENT

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text:
The practical applications of heating effect of electric current are devices and systems
that use Joule's heating (H = I^2 x R x t) for performing useful functions such as
heating, lighting, and circuit protection.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Generation of heat in a conductor is an inevitable consequence of electric current.
In many practical situations, this heat is useful (heaters, irons, bulbs).
In some situations, the heat is undesirable (power transmission losses).
KEY APPLICATIONS:
1. ELECTRIC HEATING DEVICES:
Electric laundry iron, electric toaster, electric oven, electric kettle, electric heater.
These use alloys (like Nichrome) with high resistivity.
Nichrome does not oxidise at high temperatures, making it durable.
2. ELECTRIC BULB:
Uses heating effect to produce light.
Filament must get very hot and emit light, but must not melt at such temperature.
Tungsten (melting point: 3380 degrees C) is used for making bulb filaments.
The filament is thermally isolated using insulating support.
Bulbs are filled with chemically inactive nitrogen and argon gases to prolong filament life.
Most power consumed by the bulb appears as heat; only a small part is radiated as light.
3. ELECTRIC FUSE:
One of the most important applications of Joule's heating.
Purpose: Protects circuits and appliances by stopping the flow of excessive current.
HOW IT WORKS: The fuse is placed in series with the device. It consists of a piece of
wire made of a metal or alloy (like aluminium, copper, iron, lead) with appropriate
melting point. If the current exceeds the specified value, the fuse wire heats up and
melts, breaking the circuit and stopping the flow of current.
The fuse wire is usually encased in a cartridge of porcelain or similar material with
metal ends.
Fuses for domestic purposes are rated: 1 A, 2 A, 3 A, 5 A, 10 A, etc.
Example: For an electric iron consuming 1 kW at 220 V, current = 1000/220 = 4.54 A.
A 5 A fuse must be used.
DO YOU KNOW: Many people think that electrons are consumed in an electric circuit. This
is wrong! We pay the electricity board or electric company to provide energy to move
electrons through the electric gadgets. We pay for the ENERGY consumed, not the
electrons.

items.question: Name three electrical devices based on the heating effect of electric
items.answer:
Three electrical devices based on the heating effect of electric current:
1. ELECTRIC HEATER - uses nichrome heating element to produce heat.
2. ELECTRIC BULB - tungsten filament heats up and emits light.
3. ELECTRIC FUSE - fuse wire melts to protect circuits from excess current.
Other examples: Electric iron, electric toaster, electric oven, electric kettle.

items.question: Why is tungsten used for making filaments of electric bulbs? What gases
items.answer:
WHY TUNGSTEN:
- The filament of an electric bulb must get very hot (to emit light), but must not melt.
- Tungsten has an extremely high melting point of 3380 degrees C, so it can withstand the
high temperature without melting.
- Tungsten also has a high resistivity, allowing it to heat up sufficiently with the
current flowing through it.
- It can be drawn into thin wires (high tensile strength).
GASES FILLED INSIDE:
- Bulbs are filled with chemically inactive (inert) gases: NITROGEN and ARGON.
- These gases prolong the life of the filament by preventing it from burning (oxidising).
- Without these gases, the filament would burn out quickly in the presence of air (oxygen).

items.question: What is an electric fuse? How does it work? Why is it placed in series in
items.answer:
ELECTRIC FUSE:
An electric fuse is a safety device used to protect electrical circuits and appliances
from damage caused by excessive current (short circuit or overload).

HOW IT WORKS:
- The fuse consists of a short piece of wire made of a metal or alloy (like aluminium,
copper, iron, lead, or an alloy) with an appropriate low melting point.
- It is placed in series with the device or circuit to be protected.
- Under normal conditions, the current through the fuse is within the rated limit.
- If an excessive current flows (due to a short circuit or overload), the fuse wire
heats up rapidly (H = I^2 x R x t).
- The temperature exceeds the melting point of the fuse wire.
- The fuse wire MELTS and BREAKS the circuit, stopping the flow of current.
- This protects the appliances and wiring from damage.

WHY IN SERIES:
The fuse must carry the same current as the circuit it protects. This is only possible
when it is connected in series. If connected in parallel, most current would bypass the
fuse (fuse has low resistance) and it would not protect the circuit.

RATINGS OF FUSES:
- Domestic fuses are rated: 1 A, 2 A, 3 A, 5 A, 10 A, etc.
- For a 1 kW electric iron at 220 V: I = P/V = 1000/220 = 4.54 A. Use a 5 A fuse.

items.question: Which of the following is NOT an application of the heating effect of electric current?
items.answer: C
items.explanation: An electric motor converts electrical energy into mechanical energy using the magnetic effect of current, not the heating effect. Electric heater, fuse, and bulb all use the heating effect (H = I^2 x R x t).

items.question: Why is the fuse wire made of a material with a low melting point?

options.A: So that it can carry high current
options.B: So that it melts quickly when excessive current flows, breaking the circuit
options.C: To reduce the resistance of the circuit
options.D: To increase the current in the circuit

items.answer: B
items.explanation: The fuse wire must melt and break the circuit when excessive current flows. A low melting point ensures that the fuse wire melts quickly when the current exceeds the rated value, thus protecting the circuit. High melting point material would not melt and would fail to protect.

items.question: Why are electric bulbs filled with nitrogen and argon gases?

options.A: To increase the brightness of the bulb
options.B: To reduce the temperature of the filament
options.C: To prevent the filament from burning (oxidising) and to prolong its life
options.D: To reduce the resistance of the filament

items.answer: C
items.explanation: Nitrogen and argon are chemically inactive (inert) gases. They prevent the tungsten filament from oxidising (burning out) at high temperatures, thereby prolonging the life of the filament. They do not affect brightness or temperature of the filament.

items.question: An electric iron consumes 1 kW power at 220 V. What should be the rating of the fuse to be used?
items.answer: C
items.explanation: Current = P/V = 1000/220 = 4.54 A. The fuse rating must be just above the operating current but below the damage threshold. A 5 A fuse is appropriate. A 3 A fuse would blow during normal operation; a 10 A fuse would not protect adequately.

items.question: The filament of an electric bulb is made of tungsten. What would happen if the filament were made of copper instead?

options.B: The bulb would not glow at all as copper would melt before reaching the required temperature
options.C: The bulb would work exactly the same way
options.D: The bulb would glow cooler but longer

items.answer: B
items.explanation: Copper has a melting point of only about 1085 degrees C, much lower than the temperature needed to emit light (about 2000-3000 degrees C). Copper also oxidises readily at high temperatures. So a copper filament would melt before reaching the temperature needed to emit visible light. Tungsten's melting point (3380 degrees C) makes it uniquely suitable.

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text:
Electric power is the rate at which energy is consumed or dissipated in an electric
circuit. It is also the rate at which electrical work is done.
P = VI = I^2 x R = V^2/R   ...(11.22)
The SI unit of electric power is watt (W).

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Power P = rate of doing work = rate of consumption of energy.
Using V = IR: P = VI = (IR) x I = I^2 x R
Using I = V/R: P = VI = V x (V/R) = V^2/R
Combined: P = VI = I^2 x R = V^2/R   ...(11.22)
SI unit of power: watt (W).
1 W = 1 volt x 1 ampere = 1 V A   ...(11.23)
The unit 'watt' is very small for practical use.
Larger unit: kilowatt (kW). 1 kW = 1000 W.
Electrical energy is the product of power and time.
Unit of electrical energy: watt hour (W h) or kilowatt hour (kW h).
Commercial unit of electrical energy: kilowatt hour (kW h), commonly known as 'unit'.
1 kW h = 1000 W x 3600 s = 3.6 x 10^6 W s = 3.6 x 10^6 J   ...(conversion)
MORE TO KNOW (box in textbook):
Many people think that electrons are consumed in an electric circuit. This is WRONG!
We pay the electricity board or electric company to provide ENERGY to move electrons
through the electric gadgets like bulbs, fans, engines. We pay for the ENERGY (not
electrons) that we use.
EXAMPLE 11.12:
An electric bulb is connected to a 220 V generator. The current is 0.50 A. What is
the power of the bulb?
SOLUTION: P = VI = 220 x 0.50 = 110 J/s = 110 W.
EXAMPLE 11.13:
An electric refrigerator rated 400 W operates 8 hours/day. What is the cost of energy
to operate it for 30 days at Rs 3.00 per kW h?
SOLUTION:
Total energy = 400 W x 8 h/day x 30 days = 96000 W h = 96 kW h.
Cost = 96 kW h x Rs 3.00 per kW h = Rs 288.00.
IN-TEXT QUESTIONS (after 11.8):
1. What determines the rate at which energy is delivered by a current?
2. An electric motor takes 5 A from a 220 V line. Determine the power of the motor and
the energy consumed in 2 h.
ANSWERS:
1. The rate at which energy is delivered by a current (electric power) is determined by:
The potential difference (V) across the conductor.
The current (I) flowing through the conductor.
Power P = VI. Also P = I^2 x R (depends on current and resistance) or P = V^2/R.
Power of motor: P = VI = 220 x 5 = 1100 W = 1.1 kW
Energy consumed in 2 h: E = P x t = 1100 x 7200 = 7,920,000 J = 7.92 x 10^6 J
Or in commercial units: E = 1.1 kW x 2 h = 2.2 kW h.

items.question: What is 1 kilowatt hour (kWh)? How many joules is it equal to?
items.answer:
One kilowatt hour (kWh) is the commercial unit of electric energy. It is the energy
consumed when an electrical appliance of power 1 kilowatt (1000 W) operates for 1 hour.
1 kWh = 1000 W x 3600 s = 3.6 x 10^6 J = 3,600,000 J.
This unit is also called 'unit' of electricity (used in electricity billing).

items.question: Derive the expression for electric power in terms of (a) V and I,
items.answer:
DERIVATION:
Power is defined as the rate of doing work (or rate of energy consumption):
P = W/t = H/t

From Joule's law: H = VIt   ...(11.20)
Dividing by t: P = VI   ...(Form 1)

(a) P = VI [in terms of V and I]

(b) Substituting V = IR (Ohm's law) in P = VI:
P = (IR) x I = I^2 x R   ...(Form 2)

(c) Substituting I = V/R (Ohm's law) in P = VI:
P = V x (V/R) = V^2/R   ...(Form 3)

All three forms: P = VI = I^2 x R = V^2/R   ...(11.22)

UNIT OF POWER:
1 W = 1 V x 1 A (one watt = one volt-ampere)
Larger units: 1 kW = 1000 W; 1 MW = 10^6 W.

items.question: Define electric power and commercial unit of energy. Derive P = I^2 x R.
items.answer:
ELECTRIC POWER:
Electric power is the rate at which electrical energy is consumed or dissipated in an
electric circuit.
P = VI = I^2 x R = V^2/R
Unit: watt (W). 1 W = 1 V x 1 A.

COMMERCIAL UNIT OF ENERGY:
The commercial unit of electric energy is kilowatt hour (kWh), also known as 'unit'.
1 kWh = 1000 W x 3600 s = 3.6 x 10^6 J.
This is the unit used by electricity companies for billing.

DERIVATION OF P = I^2 x R:
From Joule's law: H = VIt.
Power P = H/t = VI.
Substituting V = IR (Ohm's law): P = (IR) x I = I^2 x R.
Therefore, P = I^2 x R.

NUMERICAL:
Given: P = 2 kW = 2000 W, V = 220 V
(a) Current drawn:
P = VI => I = P/V = 2000/220 = 9.09 A
(b) Resistance:
R = V/I = 220/9.09 = 24.2 Omega
(OR: R = V^2/P = 220^2/2000 = 48400/2000 = 24.2 Omega)
(c) Energy consumed in 30 days:
Energy per day = P x t = 2 kW x 3 h = 6 kWh
Energy in 30 days = 6 x 30 = 180 kWh
Cost = 180 kWh x Rs 5 per kWh = Rs 900

items.answer: C

items.question: An electric bulb is rated 220 V and 100 W. What is the resistance of the bulb?
items.answer: B

items.question: An electric motor takes 5 A from a 220 V supply. The energy consumed in 2 hours is:
items.answer: C

items.question: Two electric bulbs, rated 40 W and 60 W respectively, are connected in series to a 220 V supply. Which bulb will glow brighter and why?

options.A: 60 W bulb, as it has lower resistance
options.B: 40 W bulb, as it has higher resistance and more power is dissipated in series
options.D: Neither glows as they are in series

items.answer: B
items.explanation: Rated at same voltage (220 V), R = V^2/P. R_40W = 220^2/40 = 1210 Omega; R_60W = 220^2/60 = 807 Omega. In series, same current flows. P = I^2 x R. More power is dissipated in the 40 W bulb (higher R), so it glows BRIGHTER in series, contrary to what the watt rating might suggest.
